Case study: Paull Holme Strays (Paull Holme Strays, Humberside, United Kingdom)
Section: CRITICAL SOURCE QUALITY NOTICE

**All four source files provided for Case ID CS53 are failed web captures of paywalled Elsevier journal articles.** The automated capture process was blocked by publisher authentication systems (CAPTCHA/403 errors). The file content consists entirely of Elsevier web analytics infrastructure code (Adobe Analytics/Adobe Experience Cloud JavaScript) and authentication challenge pages. **No substantive text from any of the four academic papers was captured or made available for analysis.**

The four intended sources are:
1. "Biogeochemical value of managed realignment, Humber estuary, UK" — DOI: 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2006.08.021 (*Science of the Total Environment*)
2. "Historical storage budgets of organic carbon, nutrient and contaminant elements in saltmarsh sediments: Biogeochemical context for managed realignment, Humber Estuary, UK" — DOI: 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2008.07.044 (*Science of the Total Environment*)
3. "Managed realignment as compensation for the loss of intertidal mudflat: A short term solution to a long term problem?" — DOI: 10.1016/j.ecss.2010.07.009 (*Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science*)
4. "Physical and biological development of a newly breached managed realignment site, Humber estuary, UK" — DOI: 10.1016/j.marpolbul.2007.09.017 (*Marine Pollution Bulletin*)

**What the source files contain:** Only Elsevier's web infrastructure code, CAPTCHA challenge pages, and HTTP error responses. No research text, abstract content, methods, results, or discussion sections were captured.

**What can be established from the source files:** Only the paper titles, DOIs, journal names, and the capture timestamps — nothing else.

**Consequence for this coding document:** The questionnaire cannot be completed from the reviewed sources. Every field below will record "No evidence found in reviewed sources." The Case Study Overview is limited to what can be responsibly stated from title-level metadata alone. No codes will be assigned. No inferences about case characteristics will be presented as coded findings.

text:
Case study: Paull Holme Strays (Paull Holme Strays, Humberside, United Kingdom)
Section: Case Study Overview

**Case Name:** Managed Realignment, Humber Estuary, United Kingdom

**Global North/South:** North (United Kingdom; supported by location in paper titles and journal metadata)

**Source limitation:** The following overview is derived exclusively from the paper titles and journal DOIs provided. No substantive content was accessible from any of the four source documents. All statements below reflect only what can be responsibly read from title-level metadata.

The four paper titles indicate that this case study concerns **managed realignment** on the **Humber Estuary** in the United Kingdom. The papers use the phrase "managed realignment" consistently — this is the standard UK coastal management term for an intervention in which coastal defence structures (typically embankments or sea walls) are deliberately modified or breached to allow tidal inundation of previously enclosed land, creating or restoring intertidal habitat. The titles cover biogeochemical aspects of the realignment (carbon, nutrients, and contaminants in saltmarsh sediments), physical and biological development at a newly breached site, and a question about whether managed realignment can adequately compensate for loss of intertidal mudflat over the long term.

The publication dates of the four papers span 2006 to 2010, suggesting that fieldwork at the site(s) studied occurred in the early-to-mid 2000s. The research appears to constitute a multi-year scientific monitoring program at one or more Humber Estuary realignment sites.

**What cannot be established from the source files:** The specific site(s) studied; the scale of the intervention; the regulatory, planning, or governance context; the trigger and decision process; funding sources; the identity of implementing agencies; whether any residential, agricultural, or other land users were displaced; and any social, equity, or community engagement dimensions.

**Plain-language narrative (for a non-technical reader):** Based on the titles of the four papers alone, this case involves a type of coastal management practice used in England in which sea walls or earthen embankments along an estuary are breached or removed, allowing the tide to reclaim land that had previously been protected. The goal, as suggested by one of the paper titles, is to create new intertidal habitat (mudflat and saltmarsh) to compensate for losses of such habitat elsewhere. The four papers study what happens after such a breach: how sediments, carbon, nutrients, and pollutants behave; how the physical and biological environment of the newly flooded area develops; and whether these newly created habitats can truly replace what was lost. One title raises the question of whether this approach is only a short-term solution to a longer-term problem, suggesting the papers engage with debates about the adequacy of managed realignment as a compensation strategy.

**Important caution:** Because no paper text was accessible, none of the above can be confirmed as describing the managed retreat decision process for this case. The papers appear to be natural science monitoring studies, not planning or governance analyses. Whether they describe a single site or multiple sites, who made the decision to realign, what the regulatory basis was, and whether people or assets were displaced cannot be determined from the titles alone.

Case study: Paull Holme Strays (Paull Holme Strays, Humberside, United Kingdom)
Section: Additional Notes and Lessons Learned

**1. Source access failure is the defining feature of this case record.** The systematic review protocol relies on automated web capture of published journal articles. For CS53, all four captures failed due to publisher authentication barriers (Elsevier's ScienceDirect paywall). The captured files contain no research content. This failure means the case study cannot be coded and should be flagged for re-capture using institutional library access, author repositories, or interlibrary loan before any coding is attempted.

**2. Nature of the case based on title-level metadata only.** The paper titles suggest that CS53 involves an ecological coastal managed realignment intervention on the Humber Estuary, UK. The papers appear to be natural science/biogeochemistry monitoring studies rather than social science, planning, or governance analyses of the retreat decision process. If this is correct, even full access to the papers might yield limited information on community engagement, compensation, governance, and socio-cultural dimensions — because those topics fall outside the apparent scope of the papers. However, this assessment is based solely on titles and cannot be confirmed.

**3. Terminology.** All four titles use "managed realignment" — the standard UK coastal management term. This is noted as metadata-level information only; no claim is made about how the case participants framed the process.

**4. Supplementary sources recommended.** If this case is to be coded, supplementary sources beyond the four identified papers would likely be needed to address social, governance, and community engagement dimensions. Relevant sources might include: UK Environment Agency documents, Humber Estuary Management Plan, relevant Shoreline Management Plans, and any planning or policy literature on the specific realignment site(s).

**5. Response to Check 1 audit.** This Version 2 document was generated entirely from scratch, with all major issues from the Check 1 audit resolved:
- All inferences that were presented too confidently in Version 1 have been removed or explicitly marked as title-only metadata observations.
- No codes have been assigned anywhere in this document, consistent with the audit finding that no code should be based on title-only inference.
- The description of the Humber Estuary as "a large tidal estuary formed by the rivers Ouse and Trent" has been removed, as this fact is not contained in the source files.
- The claim about EU Habitats Directive obligations has been removed, as it is not supported by source text.
- The claim that the case "likely involves deliberate breaching of agricultural embankments" has been removed.
- The statement that one paper "explicitly questions" the long-term adequacy of managed realignment has been replaced with the more conservative: "One title asks whether managed realignment is a short-term solution to a long-term problem."
- The internally inconsistent structure of Version 1 (stating "no evidence" then assigning "likely" codes) has been eliminated.
- The language-and-framing field has been revised to note only what appears in accessible metadata, without implying that other terms are absent from the underlying research.

**6. No disagreement with the auditor's findings.** After reviewing the source files, I confirm that all major issues identified in the Check 1 audit are valid. The Version 1 document went beyond the evidence. Version 2 corrects all identified errors.

---
